texts.preamble: Brajmohan Gupta vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 28 January, 2020 Author: Sunil Kumar Awasthi Bench: Sunil Kumar Awasthi -( 1 )- The High Court Of Madhya Pradesh Cr.R. No.3182/2017 (Brajmohan Gupta Vs. State of Madhya Pradesh) Shri Navneet Kishore Verma, learned counsel for the applicant.
texts.facts: Being aggrieved with the aforesaid judgment, this criminal revision has been preferred by the applicant. (2). The facts of the case are that on 18.09.2007, the Food Inspector K.S. Solanki visited the shop of firm Brajmohan Radhakrishna situated at Ranjeet Chowk, Badwani and purchased three bottles of 500 ML of groundnut oil and paid Rs. 120/- to the present applicant who was present at the shop at the time of inspection; sealed them at the spot and sent them to Public Analyst for examination. After examination the -( 2 )- Public Analyst disclosed that the oil was not up to the standard prescribed by the rule as given in the Apenndix-B and it described as adulterated. Thereafter, permission of prosecution was obtained from the concerned authority and complaint was filed before the Court of Judicial Magistrate First Class, Badwani. Then notice under Section 13(2) of the Act was also sent to the applicant which served upon him on 14.06.2008. (3). The applicant/accused absurd his guilt and examined himself as defence witness. Brajmohan Gupta vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 28 January, 2020 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/123613087/ 1 Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment, the applicant has preferred an appeal before the Sessions Court and same was also dismissed in toto. These orders are subject matter of challenge in the present revision petition.
texts.arguments: (5). Learned counsel for the applicant has submitted that some packed sample was collected in which the name of the manufacturer was mentioned but he has not been implicated as party in the proceedings. It is also submitted that although the report of food analyst disclosed that sample was found adulterated but no specific action of adulteration has been mentioned in the report. It is further submitted that complaint has been filed after lapse of 9 months and therefore he had deprived of his statutory right under Section 13 (2) of the Act for sent part of sample to the Central Food Laboratory for further examination. It is also submitted that if the report of the Public Analyst is accepted in its face value even then the sample was marginal away -( 3 )- from the standard and therefore it cannot be said that the sample taken from the applicant is adulterated. Under these circumstances, he prays for setting aside of the judgment of the courts below. (6). Learned counsel for the respondent/State submitted according to the Public Analyst report the sample was found to be adulterated and courts below have properly appreciated the evidence and convicted the applicant for the said offence, therefore, there is no ground is available to interfere in the concurrent findings of the courts below, hence, he prays for dismissal of the revision petition. (9). Learned counsel for the applicant has submitted that there is marginal error in the various results obtained by the Public Analyst in the sample which was examined by him and it may be compared with the standard as mentioned in the Appendix -B of the the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955 at Article A. -( 4 )- 17.03. (11). Learned counsel for the applicant has placed reliance on the judgment passed by Single Bench of this Court in the case of Ramesh Chandra Vs. State of M.P. 2014(3) M.P. H.T.382 and Beni Prasad State of M.P. 2004 (1) MPWN 201 in which there was marginal error slightly difference in the various readings between the sample and the standard fixed by the P.F. Rules, therefore, this Court was of the view that sample cannot be adulterated.
